Tie, Dye, Silicon

TLDR
  • In bandhani, tiny knots of thread keep the dye out, leaving a dot of undyed cloth behind.
  • That trick has a name: resist. Protect some places, colour the rest.
  • Microchips are made with the very same trick, called photoresist, only billions of times smaller.
  • Imagine: a bandhani dupatta whose dots are tiny lights, glowing at a garba.
  • Number to remember: how long one piece can take to tie and dye.

Then

A thousand tiny knots

Sit in a courtyard in Kutch or Jamnagar, and you'll see women working so fast their fingers blur. Each one pinches a speck of cloth, smaller than a grain of rice, and winds thread around it, tight, again and again. Then the next speck. And the next. A single fine saree can hold thousands of these little knots.

The design comes first. It's printed on the cloth with a wash of geru, red earth, often through a sheet punched with holes, so the artisans know exactly where every knot goes. A single knot is called a bindi or bheendi. Four together make a kadi, and the finest tiers are paid by the kadi.

Then the cloth goes into the dye, usually a light colour first, like yellow. Wherever the thread grips, the dye can't reach. Tie more knots, dip it in a darker colour, and repeat. Only at the very end are the threads pulled open, and the pattern appears: rings of tiny undyed dots on red, maroon or green. Tying alone can take from four days to three months, and a fine saree from six months to six years.

The craft is old. Dotted tie-dye blouses appear in the Ajanta cave paintings from around the sixth century. The poet Banabhatta described tied textiles at a royal wedding in the seventh century. The Khatri community is credited with bringing bandhani to Kutch around the twelfth century, and by the eighteenth it was a major export.

The idea underneath has a name. Dyers call it resist. You don't paint the pattern. You protect the places that must stay clean, and let the colour flood everything else.

now, imagine
Imagine

The same knot, a billion times smaller

Now shrink that idea, and shrink it again, until a dot is thousands of times thinner than a human hair. You are inside a chip factory.

A microchip starts as a thin, polished disc of silicon called a wafer. First, it's coated with a light-sensitive layer called photoresist. Yes, the same word. Then light is shone through a mask, a glass plate carrying the circuit design, like the punched sheet that marks a bandhani. Where the light lands, the resist changes. Wash it, and a pattern of protected and unprotected places appears.

Next comes the dip. Chemicals or gases eat away whatever the resist doesn't protect. Then the resist is stripped off, just like untying the knots, and a tiny pattern is left in the silicon.

And just like bandhani, it's done again and again. A new layer, a new mask, a new pattern, dozens of times over, until billions of tiny switches are stacked on a chip the size of a fingernail. The most advanced machines use extreme ultraviolet light, with a wavelength of just 13.5 nanometres, to draw the finest lines.

Try it · tie, dip, untie Everything happens in your browser

Pick a pattern and work through the five steps. Then switch to silicon: the very same steps make a layer of a chip.

This whole pattern, drawn at real chip scale, would fit under a fingernail. These squares are enlarged about a hundred and fifty times.

There's a lovely coincidence. Gujarat, home of bandhani, is also where India's first big chip factory is being built, at Dholera, by Tata Electronics with Taiwan's PSMC. The same state that perfected the knot is learning to tie it in silicon.

Turn a finished chip over and you'll find another surprise. Its underside is a field of tiny metal dots that connect it to the circuit board. Hold it next to an opened bandhani, and the two look like cousins.

And the story can come full circle, back to cloth. Google named its smart-clothing project Jacquard, after the loom in our last story, and wove touch-sensitive threads into a denim jacket made with Levi's. Now imagine a bandhani dupatta where each tied dot is a tiny light. At a garba, the dots glow brighter as the dancers spin faster. The knot that once said no dye here now says light here.

The oldest trick in the dyer's courtyard turned out to be the most important trick in electronics: protect what matters, and change everything else.

StoryboardKnots of light, in seven panels

In a Kutch courtyard, women tie knots at lightning speed. One more knot!

At the dye vats, the dyer lifts a dripping dupatta and the goat sneezes. Yellow first, red later.

On the rooftop, the cloth is pulled open with a snap, and thousands of tiny dots appear.

In a chip factory, workers in white suits handle shining wafers.

A technician holds up a wafer of chips. Same idea, smaller knots!

Under the microscope, the chip looks just like bandhani. I tied that, says the grandmother.

At the garba, bandhani glows as the dancers spin. Knots of light.
